meta.title: Towards Robust and Efficient Multispectral Change Detection

abstract: Objective: Multispectral change detection (CD) supports environmental monitoring and autonomous Earth observation, but onboard models must remain reliable under acquisition variation while satisfying tight compute and memory constraints. Existing OOD work in Earth observation primarily emphasizes detection or uncertainty estimation rather than improving the intrinsic robustness of lightweight CD models. Methods: We introduce Head-Consistency Adversarial Training (HCAT), a lightweight objective that stabilizes pixelwise decision margins under physically structured radiometric, illumination, calibration, and optical perturbations. The perturbations are evaluated over ordinary, development-calibrated, extrapolated, and composed severity regimes. HCAT changes only training and adds no inference-time parameters or computation. Results: Across three pretrained OSCD architectures, HCAT improves activated-shift F1 over matched physical augmentation by 0.035–0.043 and over the corresponding untreated models by 0.093–0.339. On a larger 2,400-pair held-out SYSU-CD replication, activated-shift macro-F1 reaches 0.611, versus 0.548 for physical augmentation and 0.250 for standard training. A six-pair CropRot probe shows that acquisition robustness does not automatically imply semantic-domain transfer. Conclusion and Significance: Decision-margin stabilization provides a practical mechanism for improving acquisition-shift robustness across CD models of substantially different capacities while preserving their original inference graph.

blocks.html: Change detection (CD) from multi-temporal satellite imagery supports disaster response, deforestation monitoring, urban expansion analysis, and agricultural intelligence [1– 3]. As Earth observation platforms move toward increasing autonomy, onboard interpretation of multispectral imagery can reduce downlink bandwidth, shorten response time, and enable adaptive sensing [4, 5]. Such deployment, however, requires models that are not only accurate and computationally efficient but also reliable under acquisition variations such as illumination, calibration, and optical changes.

Modern CD systems are dominated by encoder–decoder and Siamese architectures [6, 7], with increasingly expressive attention, transformer, and foundation-scale models improving representation capacity [8–12]. Their computational footprints can conflict with onboard constraints, while high clean accuracy alone does not ensure stability under distribution shift. Conversely, Earth-observation OOD research has largely emphasized detecting unfamiliar inputs or estimating uncertainty [13, 14], rather than improving the intrinsic resistance of compact dense CD models.

We consider the pixelwise decision margin as a direct target for such robustness. A binary CD prediction ultimately depends on the relative change/no-change logits at each pixel; a structured acquisition shift changes the decision only when this ordering is reversed. Based on this observation, we introduce Head-Consistency Adversarial Training (HCAT), which encourages the class favored by the clean model to retain a positive margin under deliberately challenging, physically structured radiometric, illumination, calibration, and optical perturbations. HCAT requires one clean and one shifted evaluation during training, introduces no iterative inner maximization, and leaves the inference architecture unchanged.

We evaluate HCAT on three established OSCD checkpoints spanning approximately 0.54M–34.9M parameters, with matched clean fine-tuning, physical augmentation, and PGD-AT controls. Across all three architectures, HCAT improves activated-shift F1 over matched physical augmentation by 0.035–0.043, with the advantage persisting under extrapolated and composed shifts. A larger SYSU-CD experiment reproduces the same ordering, whereas a six-pair CropRot probe shows that acquisition robustness does not automatically imply semantic-domain generalization. The resulting scope is therefore deliberately focused: improving acquisition-shift robustness of deployable CD models without claiming general OOD invariance.

Change detection and onboard inference. Early deep CD systems established convolutional encoder–decoder and Siamese processing as effective alternatives to conventional image-difference pipelines [6, 7]. U-Net-style models preserve multi-scale spatial detail through encoder– decoder skip connections [15], while attention-gated and transformer-based variants increase contextual modeling capacity [8–10]. Bridging these approaches, TinyCD [16] leverages a lightweight Siamese U-Net with economical spatio-temporal feature mixing and attention, achieving competitive CD performance with substantially lower model and computational complexity. More recently, remote-sensing foundation models such as SatMAE and SpectralGPT have demonstrated the benefits of large-scale spectral–spatial pretraining [11, 12]. These developments improve representation power, but larger attention and foundation-scale models remain difficult to reconcile with the memory, energy, and latency budgets of orbital edge platforms [4, 5]. Our evaluation therefore deliberately spans both sub-million-parameter models and a substantially larger Siam-Swin-UNet (SS-UNet) [9].

Robustness and OOD in Earth observation. Existing OOD studies in remote sensing primarily address recognition of unfamiliar samples or predictive uncertainty [13, 14]. Formal robustness methods instead seek guarantees within prescribed perturbation sets [17–19], with recent extensions to dense segmentation and detection [20–22]. However, bitemporal multispectral inputs and dense outputs make such verification difficult to scale for CD. Empirical adversarial training is more tractable, but conventional norm-bounded perturbations do not directly represent the smooth spatial, band-dependent, and optical variation encountered in multispectral acquisition. This motivates evaluating robustness under structured acquisition shifts rather than treating all input variation through a single generic perturbation norm.

Positioning this work. HCAT lies between these two directions. It is not an OOD detector and does not provide a formal certificate; instead, it improves empirical prediction stability by regularizing the final pixelwise margin under physically structured stress tests. Unlike direct physical augmentation, HCAT does not supervise every shifted pixel toward its ground-truth class, but asks the shifted prediction to preserve the decision supported by the clean observation. Unlike iterative PGD-based training, it requires no input-gradient search. This makes HCAT complementary to stronger CD architectures and OOD-detection mechanisms: its specific objective is to add acquisition-shift resistance without increasing inference-time model size or computation.

We first describe the evaluation architectures, followed by (i) the structured acquisition-shift benchmark, (ii) the pixelwise decision-margin formulation, and (iii) Head- Consistency Adversarial Training (HCAT), which stabilizes these margins without changing the inference architecture.

For the OSCD study, we evaluate HCAT on three established dense CD baselines with substantially different capacities. All three models receive the two 13-band Sentinel- 2 dates through early fusion and predict two change/nochange logits per pixel. TinyCD [16] serves as our tiny baseline, utilizing a lightweight Siamese U-Net with economical spatio-temporal feature mixing and attention. FresUNet is a compact, small-capacity U-Net-style encoder– decoder architecture characterized by channel widths of 8–16–32–64–128, residual skip connections, and nearestneighbor upsampling, as introduced alongside the OSCD dataset [6]. Finally, as a high-capacity baseline, SS-UNet blends a Siamese architecture, a U-Net encoder–decoder structure, and Swin Transformer blocks, offering a substantial parameter footprint of 34.9M for remote-sensing change detection.

Multispectral Sentinel-2 imagery exhibits two forms of distribution shift that strongly affect change detection performance: (i) radiometric or optical variations across acquisitions, and (ii) semantic and temporal shift driven by vegetation dynamics. We explicitly model both regimes to construct a compact preliminary robustness benchmark tailored to multispectral change detection. Radiometric perturbations. Satellite acquisition variation may be spatially structured, band dependent, and different across the two temporal observations. We represent each co-registered image pair using all 13 Sentinel-2 bands at both dates, scaled to reflectance-like values in [0, 1]. Sentinel-2 acquisition differs fundamentally from conventional RGB imagery through its multispectral, band-dependent radiometric and spatial characteristics [23]. Generic corruption suites such as ImageNet-C [24] provide an important reference for robustness to common RGB corruptions, but do not capture the bitemporal and band-specific structure of multispectral change detection.

We therefore introduce four perturbation families aligned with representative acquisition effects. Let xt,b(u, v) denote band b at spatial location (u, v) and date t ∈{1, 2}. The transformations are applied independently to the two dates and clipped to [0, 1]:
1. smooth additive low-frequency drift,

3. per-band affine calibration variation,
representing gain, offset, and spectral-response mismatch;
4. Gaussian blur with standard deviation σ, representing degradation in effective spatial resolution.

The functional forms are motivated by radiometric, illumination, calibration, and optical variation in multispectral acquisition. Their amplitudes are treated as controlled benchmark severities rather than as a complete probabilistic model of Sentinel-2 sensor error. This distinction also separates the proposed acquisition-shift benchmark from a generic norm-bounded adversarial threat model.

For each perturbation family, the selected multiplier is the setting closest to an 8% clean-to-perturbed pixel-decision flip rate while retaining at least 55% of the clean development F1. This procedure selects a multiplier of 1.5 for drift and 2.5 for illumination, calibration, and blur. The official OSCD test labels are never used during this selection.

We refer to the resulting settings as activated shifts. To test behavior beyond the selected severity, we further evaluate 1.25× extrapolations and two composed perturbations: drift with calibration variation, and illumination variation with blur. The activated, extrapolated, and composed regimes are explicitly treated as controlled robustness stress tests rather than estimates of routine sensor noise. In contrast, standard norm-bounded robustness is evaluated separately using an ℓ∞PGD-based baseline.

Figure 1 provides a visual reference for the activated operating point. The examples illustrate the distinct spatial, radiometric, spectral, and optical character of the four shift families; the same operators, at different amplitudes, define the ordinary and extrapolated regimes. CropRot protocol. CropRot provides a preliminary semantic-transfer probe using six co-registered Sentinel-2 Level-2A pairs from agricultural regions in Iowa. All pairs are evaluation-only. Vegetation-change masks are obtained from thresholded temporal NDVI difference, NDVI = (B8 −B4)/(B8 + B4), followed by a visual alignment check. No CropRot image is used for training, checkpoint selection, threshold selection, or perturbation calibration. SYSU-CD scale replication. To test whether the central OSCD robustness ordering persists at larger sample size, we use the available 12,000-pair SYSU-CD RGB training subset with a deterministic 7,200/2,400/2,400 train/validation/test split. For this RGB experiment, we instantiate the FresUNet family described in Section 3.1 with six-channel T1/T2 RGB input. Standard is trained first; after a predeclared cleanperformance gate, PhysAug and HCAT are initialized from the same Standard checkpoint. The OSCD-selected perturbation scales are frozen without SYSU-specific recalibration. Evaluation is deliberately restricted to clean, the four activated single-family shifts, and the two composed shifts, making this a scale-oriented replication rather than a second full factorial study. The internal pair-level split is not treated as the official SYSU-CD benchmark.

For OSCD, all fine-tuned branches start from the same audited checkpoint and use five epochs, identical 128×128 patch ordering and geometric augmentation, Adam with learning rate 5 × 10−5, and weight decay 10−4. PhysAug and HCAT receive identical sampled full-scene perturbations, whose strength is ramped over the first 25% of training. HCAT therefore requires one clean and one shifted forward pass but no iterative input-gradient search, and leaves inference unchanged.

We first reproduced three established OSCD checkpoints using their original 13-band preprocessing and 128×128 fullscene reconstruction, obtaining clean F1 of 0.518, 0.610, and 0.579 for FresUNet, SS-UNet, and TinyCD. All fine-tuned branches use the corresponding checkpoint and matched optimization. Table 1 summarizes full-scene results and Fig. 2 the severity progression.

Clean OSCD. HCAT shows the expected clean– robustness trade-off, with clean F1 decreasing relative to Vanilla, but remaining above PhysAug for all three architectures. Clean-FT performs substantially worse than HCAT under activated shifts, confirming that the robustness gain is not explained by additional fine-tuning alone.

Radiometric OOD. HCAT improves activated F1 over Vanilla for all three architectures and, more importantly, exceeds the matched PhysAug control by 0.035–0.043 F1, isolating the benefit of margin regularization from perturbation exposure. The advantage persists under extrapolated and composed shifts. PGD-AT instead becomes strongly precision-biased, with clean recall falling to 0.066–0.167 and correspondingly poor F1. This behavior is specific to the tested three-step norm-bounded configuration and should not be interpreted as a general limitation of adversarial training.

CropRot (semantic OOD). CropRot reveals strong architecture dependence rather than consistent semantic transfer. Only the untouched SS-UNet transfers nontrivially (F1 0.364), and OSCD robustness fine-tuning does not preserve this behavior. Thus, acquisition-shift robustness should not be interpreted as general semantic-OOD robustness; CropRot is retained only as a preliminary external diagnostic. SYSU-CD scale replication. The reduced SYSU experiment compares Standard, PhysAug, and HCAT on the same compact RGB encoder–decoder under clean, four activated, and two composed conditions. HCAT attains macro-F1 0.656/0.611/0.553 on clean/activated/composed inputs, versus 0.643/0.250/0.267 for Standard and 0.652/0.548/0.518 for PhysAug. Thus, the larger-sample experiment reproduces the central OSCD ordering while remaining a targeted scale replication, not a full severity study, official SYSU-CD benchmark, or cross-region test.

We introduced HCAT, a training-only objective that improves multispectral CD robustness by stabilizing the pixelwise decision margin under structured acquisition shifts. Across three OSCD architectures initialized from pretrained checkpoints, HCAT consistently outperforms matched physical augmentation under activated, extrapolated, and composed perturbations without changing inference cost, and the same ordering is reproduced in a larger SYSU-CD scale experiment. The tested PGD-AT configuration transfers poorly to these shifts, while CropRot shows that acquisition robustness does not imply semantic-domain generalization. The remaining limitations—small OSCD scene count, synthetic stress tests, an internal SYSU split, and a compact semantic probe—motivate future region-disjoint multispectral evaluation under naturally occurring acquisition shifts.

The OSCD and SYSU-CD datasets are publicly available from their original authors. CropRot is derived from publicly accessible Sentinel-2 Level-2A imagery. Preprocessing scripts and evaluation splits will be made publicly available to support reproducibility.
